doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: George Shearing's locked-hand style and his reluctance to change
summary: She says Shearing's block-chord style influenced everyone but that she moved on; he has not changed much, though he wants to explore freer playing when they work together.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: How much . . . I know you said publically how much an influence George Shearing’s been on you, but how much of an influence has you been on George Shearing?

I don’t think George has been that much of an influence on me, truthfully, except of course everybody, when he first started, everybody liked to play his two-hand, his locked-hand things. I still like to do that, but not as much as I used to years ago. I used to like to do that. I still do it, but not in the same way. Not with the same chords, because after hearing . . .
Phineas and a lot of others.
. . . the way a lot of other people play. George still . . . He hasn’t really moved much from either side, has he? He . . .
I don’t think so, but that’s just my humble opinion as well.

He had the group, and that was one sound. Now he’s doing the same sound with a duo. He hasn’t really . . . I don’t think he’s changed much, although he does like to . . . he does . . . whenever he and I work together, he wants to do a free thing or get into some . . .
. . . other areas, and he can do it. He can do it.

I think sometimes artists get to that point where they almost feel that they, they’re almost imitating themselves. They’re afraid to move out of that area, because they’re so well known for certain devices or whatever.

That is true of George, and he admitted it, that he was afraid to break up the quintet, because he would . . . people were so used to that sound. He went through that, of making himself break up the quintet, and I think he probably a reached a peak of performance and being known by the public that it didn’t matter whether he played solo or duo or what he did. It seems that he was well established, so he could do his own thing. At least that’s my feeling. Because that’s what he wants to do, is play . . . He likes to play with a symphony orchestra. I know he likes to have something written by Robert Farnon. And he did a couple of other things with some other groups, but mostly he does his own thing.
